# Introduction

Which visit should a decision tree use? Keeping just the last visit gives
one row per patient, so it is easy to fit an ordinary classification or
regression tree (CART) [@breiman1984cart]. The price is that the tree never
sees the earlier tests. Averaging over visits loses a different piece of
information: the same average bilirubin can come from a rise or a fall.

A Time-penalized Tree (TpT) [@valla2024tpt] can ask a question such as
"Was albumin below this threshold at visit 4?" The visit is part of the
split, just like the threshold. A later visit can beat an earlier one
only if its gain makes up for the extra penalty. If the requested visit
is absent, the split can send the patient to a separate terminal branch.

We show how to fit and read these trees in `scikit-longitudinal` (Sklong),
the Python library introduced by @provost2025sklong. The integration adds
classification and regression estimators, the compiled split rule, and an
export that shows the visits used by the tree. We work through one example
from a Mayo Clinic trial: given the first five years of follow-up, does
keeping all recorded visits help distinguish patients who die or undergo
liver transplantation by year ten?

Within Sklong, lexicographic splitting also works with measurements from
different visits, but breaks near-ties in favor of the more recent ones
[@ribeiro2024lexico]. TpT favors earlier visits when their gains are close.
This choice serves a different purpose from using a tree to find changes
in model parameters [@zeileis2008mob; @seibold2019glmtrees], modeling
within-subject dependence with random effects [@sela2012reem;
@hajjem2014merf], or fitting a censored time-to-event outcome [@fu2017ltrc].

# The TpT split rule

## Prediction target

In the general formulation [@valla2026consistency], both the predictors
$X_i(t)$ and the response $Y_i(t)$ can change with time for subject $i$.
Write $X_{i0}$ for the duration of observation and
$\mathcal I(t)=\{i:X_{i0}\ge t\}$ for the subjects still under observation
at $t$. The regression target at time $t$ is
$m_t(X_{\le t})=\mathbb E[Y(t)\mid X_{\le t}]$, where
$X_{\le t}=\{X(s):s\le t\}$ is the history available by $t$. For a binary
response, this is the probability $\Pr\{Y(t)=1\mid X_{\le t}\}$. The
theoretical result below concerns a fixed-time subtree, with target
$f_t^\star(x)=\mathbb E[Y(t)\mid X(t)=x,A_t]$. Here $A_t$ means that the
subject remains under observation at $t$ and reaches the subtree by
following the earlier split rules.

The Python estimators take **one response per subject**. In the case
study, we give each patient a single label $Z_i$ for a future event after
a common prediction date $L$. We estimate $\Pr(Z=1\mid X_{\le L})$ by
routing each patient to a leaf and reporting the fraction of training
patients there who had the event. Two patients can reach their leaves
using different visits, but the outcome window is the same for both.

## Impurity and the duration branch

Impurity measures how mixed the outcomes are within a node. In
classification, impurity is zero when everyone has the same outcome
and highest when the classes are equally frequent. Renaming the classes
leaves it unchanged. If $p_k(g)$ is the proportion of class $k$ in node
$g$, the Gini and entropy criteria are

$$
I_{\mathrm{Gini}}(g)=1-\sum_{k=1}^K p_k(g)^2,\qquad
I_{\mathrm{Ent}}(g)=-\sum_{k=1}^K p_k(g)\log_2 p_k(g),
$$

with $0\log_2 0=0$. For regression, mean squared error is
$I_{\mathrm{MSE}}(g)=|g|^{-1}\sum_{i\in g}(y_i-\bar y_g)^2$, where
$\bar y_g$ is the node mean.

Start at a parent node that has reached wave $t_p$ (wave 0 at the root).
A candidate split tests a threshold $b$ on a measurement $X_j(t_c)$ at
wave $t_c\ge t_p$. Subjects with that visit can go left or right. Those
whose records end before $t_c$ can go to a third child, the **duration
leaf**. Its prediction comes from training subjects with the same routing
history and no measurement at the requested visit.

Write $g_\ell$, $g_r$ and $g_d$ for these three children of node $g$.
Subtract their size-weighted impurity from the impurity of $g$, then
discount the gain for advancing from $t_p$ to $t_c$. The score is

$$
G_\gamma(g;j,b,t_c)=
\left[I(g)-\sum_{h\in\{g_\ell,g_r,g_d\}}\frac{|h|}{|g|}I(h)\right]
\exp[-\gamma(t_c-t_p)],
$$

where an empty child contributes zero. TpT takes the admissible split with
the highest positive score. Without a duration child, the gain in brackets
is the usual CART impurity decrease. Setting $\gamma=0$ removes the discount
but still requires visits to come in order along a branch. Raising $\gamma$
gives earlier visits more weight in the split search.

## Scope of the theoretical guarantee

The consistency result of @valla2026consistency is about the subtrees
that a growing TpT actually forms. Their regression analysis uses
TpT-$\alpha$, which requires each ordinary child to keep at least a
fraction $\alpha$ of the parent's observations. The proof follows
*record-high times*, where the best penalized gain exceeds the gains at all
later times. A1 requires a positive gap above the later competitors. A2
requires the empirical gain peaks at those times and at their best later
competitors to approach the corresponding envelope values as the node
grows.

**Theorem 1 (Valla and Milhaud, 2026).** Suppose A1 and A2 hold, the
TpT-$\alpha$ rule is used, and the fixed-time target has the conditional
bounded-variation approximation and sub-Gaussian noise conditions used in
the CART oracle bound [@klusowski2024cart]. Fix a record-high time $t_k$
with positive probability of continued observation. If the $t_k$-subtree
forms with probability tending to one and the approximation and variance
terms in the oracle bound converge to zero in $L^1$, then

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[
\|\widehat f_{t_k,K(t_k)}-f_{t_k}^\star\|^2_{L^2(P^{(t_k)}_{X(t_k)})}
\right]\longrightarrow 0,
$$

where $K(t_k)$ is the selected subtree depth and $P^{(t_k)}_{X(t_k)}$ is the
law of $X(t_k)$ given $A_{t_k}$. This is the fixed-time regression guarantee
in Theorem 2 of @valla2026consistency. The case study below uses a
fixed-depth classifier to illustrate the software.

# Software and reproducibility

The published library installs with `python -m pip install scikit-longitudinal`.
Use [`LongitudinalDataset.to_wide`](https://scikit-longitudinal.readthedocs.io/latest/tutorials/long_wide_reshape/)
to put each patient on one row. Pass the resulting matrix and
`features_group`, which gives the columns for each predictor in visit
order, to `TpTDecisionTreeClassifier` or `TpTDecisionTreeRegressor`.
Set `gamma` to control the penalty and `criterion` to choose the impurity.
`max_depth` and `min_samples_leaf` control tree size. A duration leaf can
be smaller than the minimum set for the ordinary leaves.

The Python estimators pass the visit groups and penalty to the Cython
splitter and tree builder in `scikit-lexicographical-trees`. The compiled
code handles the repeated work of sorting feature columns and scoring
thresholds. For a fixed number of classes, a fit costs at most
$O(Dpn\log n)$ at depth $D$ with $n$ observations and $p$ candidate
feature-wave columns. Trying another penalty means fitting another tree.

The visit order along a branch is a constraint on *when* a split can
look. It does not constrain how predictions change as a predictor's
value rises. TpT does not implement that second constraint: if a caller
sets `monotonic_cst`, the estimator warns and disables it.

**Backend for the case study.** In release 0.0.5, a duration leaf can pick
up counts from a losing candidate, and a training partition can differ
from the routing used at prediction. We build that release with a local
correction that keeps records with absent visits out of the ordinary
branches and restores the winning split's partition and duration
statistics. We check each fitted tree by sending the training records
through it again and comparing the observed leaf counts and class
proportions with the stored ones. The correction is specific to the
article and to absent trailing visits.

The [article repository](https://github.com/MathiasValla/scikit-longitudinal-tpt)
contains the data snapshot, the analysis code and the build helper. The
helper checks the backend archive against its checksum before patching
and compiling it. From the checkout, with Conda, Quarto and LaTeX
available, run:

```bash
bash scripts/reproduce.sh
```

The script recreates the environment and renders the paper in HTML and
PDF. The environment file pins Python 3.11 and the Sklong revision and
lists the tools needed to compile the extension. The Sklong release notes
credit Mathias Valla for the TpT integration. Simon Provost and Alex
Freitas are the authors of the original library [@provost2025sklong].

# Case study: predicting death or transplant from earlier visits {#sec-case-study}

## Cohort and outcome

The public `pbcseq` data contain 1,945 visits for the 312 randomized
participants in a Mayo Clinic trial on primary biliary cholangitis
[@dataset-pbcseq]. The trial scheduled follow-up at six months, one year
and annually thereafter, and the records also include extra visits. We
use four measurements available at every visit in our analysis: serum
bilirubin (`bili`), serum albumin (`albumin`), prothrombin time (`protime`)
and aspartate aminotransferase (`ast`).

Take year five after enrolment (day 1,826) as the prediction date.
From the visits recorded by then, we predict whether a patient will die
or receive a liver transplant by year ten (day 3,652). Let $T_i$ be the
observed follow-up time in days and let $\delta_i$ be 0 for censoring, 1
for transplant and 2 for death. The binary label is

$$
Z_i=\mathbf 1\{1826<T_i\le 3652,\ \delta_i\in\{1,2\}\}.
$$

To know the label, we need $T_i>1826$ and either a recorded event or
observation through day 3,652. We exclude 110 patients whose follow-up
ended by year five and 94 more who were censored before year ten. The
remaining 108 patients have 57 events and 51 observed non-events in the
window. This complete-endpoint restriction determines whom the comparison
describes; it does not adjust for censoring.

We retain 621 visits through year five, between one and seven per
patient (median six). We number each patient's visits from zero.
Visit index 2 means the third recorded visit, whenever it occurred
(@tbl-pbc-preview). In the wide table, the columns beyond a patient's
last visit stay empty. Those shorter histories give the tree a chance
to use a duration leaf.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-pbc-preview
#| tbl-cap: "Four visits from one eligible patient. Day counts days since enrolment; wave is the recorded visit index, starting at 0. TpT uses the visit index, not the number of days between tests."
#| tbl-colwidths: [12, 12, 19, 19, 19, 19]
import numpy as np
from IPython.display import HTML, display
from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
from analysis.tpt_case_study import (
    BIOMARKERS, auc_summary, fit_tpt, load_cohort,
    plot_roc, plot_tpt, run_cv, tree_summary,
)

cohort = load_cohort()
preview = cohort.visits.loc[cohort.visits.id.eq(cohort.visits.id.iloc[0])]
display(HTML(preview[["day", "wave", *BIOMARKERS]].head(4).round(2).to_html(index=False)))
```

## Fit and evaluate

What does the model gain by seeing earlier tests? We give all trees
the same four biomarkers. TpT sees every visit through year five; CART
sees only each patient's last available visit. That last row comes
from different visits for different patients. To see whether knowing
when that row was recorded is enough, we also fit CART with its visit
index and elapsed day.

All three fits use entropy, at most three levels of splits and at least
20 patients in each ordinary leaf. We use $\gamma=0.1$ to illustrate a
nonzero time penalty. Here is one fold of the analysis, from reshaping
the visit records to scoring the outcome for held-out patients.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
from scikit_longitudinal.data_preparation import LongitudinalDataset
from scikit_longitudinal.estimators.trees import TpTDecisionTreeClassifier
from analysis.tpt_case_study import BIOMARKERS, GAMMA, PARAMS, load_cohort

cohort = load_cohort()
long = cohort.visits[["id", "wave", *BIOMARKERS]]
dataset = LongitudinalDataset(file_path=None, data_frame=long)
X = dataset.to_wide(
    id_col="id", time_col="wave", longitudinal_columns=BIOMARKERS,
    wave_format="{feature}_t{wave}",
)
groups = dataset.feature_groups()
train, test = next(StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0
).split(X, cohort.y))
model = TpTDecisionTreeClassifier(features_group=groups, gamma=GAMMA, **PARAMS)
model.fit(X.iloc[train], cohort.y[train])
event_score = model.predict_proba(X.iloc[test])[:, 1]
```

We split by patient, using the same stratified five-fold partition for
all three models. Within a repeat, each patient is scored by a model
trained on the other four folds. We pool those 108 scores to compute
the area under the ROC curve (AUC). We use ten partitions, with seeds
0 through 9. @fig-pbc-roc shows the curves for the first repeat and
the paired AUC difference for every repeat. @tbl-pbc-auc gives the
summaries for all three models.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-pbc-roc
#| fig-cap: "Predicting death or transplant by year ten. (a) ROC curves from the first five-fold repeat, with pooled out-of-fold AUCs in the legend. The dotted diagonal marks chance discrimination. CART with timing also uses the last visit's index and elapsed day. (b) TpT AUC minus last-visit CART AUC in each repeat, on identical patient folds. The dashed line marks the mean difference."
#| fig-alt: "The first-repeat ROC has AUC 0.838 for TpT and 0.720 for last-visit CART. Across the ten repeats, each paired AUC difference favors TpT."
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-pos: H
predictions, aucs = run_cv(cohort)
plot_roc(predictions[0], aucs)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-pbc-auc
#| tbl-cap: "Mean and range of out-of-fold ROC AUC across the ten shared five-fold partitions. The range describes variation with the partition, not a confidence interval."
#| tbl-colwidths: [39, 21, 20, 20]
display(HTML(auc_summary(aucs).to_html(index=False, float_format="{:.3f}".format)))
```

Across the ten repeats, TpT's AUC is between 0.053 and 0.128 higher than
that of last-visit CART. Giving CART the timing of its last visit does
not close the gap in this cohort. In the first repeat, duration leaves
give the final score for 17 held-out patients.

We explored different prediction windows and settings on this cohort
before settling on the example. Some earlier windows favored CART.
The paired comparisons show what happens when we repartition these
patients; a separate cohort would be needed to test how well the result
carries over.

## Read the exported tree

To read the rules, we refit the tree on all 108 patients and draw it
with `plot_tree` (@fig-pbc-tree). The ROC curves above use out-of-fold
scores. Start with a patient whose record ends at visit index 3. The
tree asks for albumin at index 4 and
finds no such visit. The patient follows the dashed branch: 11 of the
14 training patients in that leaf had an event. There is no need to
substitute albumin from an earlier visit. For a patient whose albumin
at index 4 exceeds 3.415, the next question uses bilirubin at index 5.
That rule has its own duration leaf for patients whose records end
at index 4.

The two full-cohort fits have different shapes. TpT has
depth two, three ordinary leaves and two duration leaves. Last-visit
CART has depth three and four ordinary leaves. It also splits on albumin
first (threshold 3.215) and bilirubin next, but each rule uses the last
available value, regardless of which visit supplied it. Prothrombin time
and AST were available to both trees and win no split in either refit.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-pbc-tree
#| fig-cap: "TpT refitted to all 108 patients. With the requested visit present, follow a solid arrow. If the record stops before that visit, take the dashed branch. Leaves show the event percentage and fraction (events/patients). Blue and ochre indicate event and no-event majorities in ordinary leaves. The axis marks the visit index reached at the node (0 at the root); vertical spacing is schematic."
#| fig-alt: "Albumin at visit index 4 leads to an event proportion of 11 of 14 when that visit is absent. The branch above the albumin threshold tests bilirubin at index 5 and routes one event in three patients to its duration leaf when the visit is absent."
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-pos: H
rows = np.arange(len(cohort.y))
fitted = fit_tpt(cohort, rows)
assert tree_summary(fitted) == {
    "split_waves": [4, 5], "ordinary_leaves": 3,
    "duration_leaves": 2, "duration_patients": 17,
}
plot_tpt(fitted, cohort.wide.columns)
plt.show()
```

With the same patients and depth limit, raising $\gamma$ to 0.3 shifts
the splits from visits 4 and 5 to visits 1, 2 and 3. This is the practical
effect of the penalty here: the tree asks for earlier measurements.

# Discussion

The exported tree lets us trace a prediction to the visits it uses.
For a shorter record, we can also see which visit was absent and how
many comparable training patients contributed to the prediction. The
AUC comparison combines two differences: the split rule and the
information available to it. We cannot tell from this comparison how
much of the gap comes from earlier biomarker values and how much
from the pattern of recorded visits.

For this application, the next question is how the comparison changes
when patients with censored outcomes can contribute to the evaluation,
using survival-specific metrics. On the software side, we would first
test duration routing more broadly. Individual paths through an exported
tree would help show why a patient reached a particular leaf. The same
splitter could also be used in ensembles or given a penalty that reflects
prior knowledge about lags between predictors and responses.
